subsection: 5. The Civil War, state building and the consolidation of democracy, 1922–1932

notes.h: Background: the Treaty, dominion status and the republic
notes.b: The Civil War grew out of a quarrel over the Anglo-Irish Treaty. To follow the fighting you need to know what the Treaty gave, what it withheld, and why two sides formed around it.
points: The Treaty, signed on 6 December 1921, gave Ireland dominion status (self-government within the Commonwealth, as Canada had), an oath to the Crown, British retention of three ports, and partition, because Northern Ireland could opt out and a Boundary Commission would fix the border.

The Dáil (the Irish parliament) approved the Treaty by 64 votes to 57 on 7 January 1922. De Valera resigned as President of the Dáil on 9 January, and Griffith was elected in his place on 10 January 1922.
The War of Independence (1919-21) had ended in a truce in July 1921. The IRA had fought it as the army of the Dáil, so when the Dáil split, the army's loyalty was also in question.
Pro-Treaty leaders argued that dominion status gave the 'freedom to achieve freedom': a self-governing state that could win more independence step by step.
A republic, the form of state the anti-Treaty side demanded, means a state with no king and no Crown. Anti-Treaty supporters therefore rejected the oath and the Crown as a betrayal of that aim.
The argument was mainly over the oath and the Crown, that is, republic against dominion status, and not mainly over partition.
notes.tip: Keep this recall to a line or two in an answer. Examiners want the Civil War dated and explained, not a re-run of the Treaty debates.

notes.h: Two authorities and a divided IRA, January-April 1922
notes.b: After the Dáil vote, Ireland had two rival governments and two armies in the making. The split in the IRA turned a political quarrel into a military one.
points: The Provisional Government took office in January 1922 with Collins as chairman, and took over Dublin Castle from the British on 16 January. Collins was also Minister for Finance.
Griffith led the Dáil government, so for five months two authorities existed side by side, each claiming to speak for the Irish people.
A new National Army was recruited from early 1922 under Mulcahy, who was Minister for Defence and chief of staff. Mulcahy, not Collins, ran the army as it was built up.

Anti-Treaty IRA officers held a convention on 26 March 1922 and rejected the authority of the Dáil. Rory O'Connor and Liam Lynch were their leaders, and Lynch became chief of staff of the anti-Treaty IRA.
British troops handed over barracks from January 1922, and both pro- and anti-Treaty forces took them over, which led to local clashes.

On 14 April 1922 the anti-Treaty IRA under Rory O'Connor occupied the Four Courts in Dublin and held it as a headquarters. This occupation was a challenge to the government, but it was not the start of the fighting.
notes.tip: Do not date the start of the Civil War from the Four Courts occupation in April. The fighting began on 28 June 1922, and examiners warn about this common error.

notes.h: From the pact to the Four Courts, May-June 1922
notes.b: In the weeks before the election, both sides tried to avoid war, but a series of events in June pushed the government into attacking the Four Courts.
points: The Collins-de Valera pact of 20 May 1922 proposed a joint Sinn Féin panel of pro- and anti-Treaty candidates. Collins repudiated it in mid-June, just before the poll.
In the general election of 16 June 1922 pro-Treaty candidates won 58 seats and anti-Treaty candidates 36. Labour won 17, and the remainder went to Farmers and independents.
The draft Constitution was published on the morning of the poll, so voters could see the form the new state would take. The Dáil did not meet until September 1922.
On 22 June 1922 two IRA men, Reginald Dunne and Joseph O'Sullivan, shot Sir Henry Wilson, a unionist MP and security adviser to the Northern government, in London.
The British government pressed Collins to act against the Four Courts garrison.
On 26 June 1922 the Four Courts garrison kidnapped J.J. ‘Ginger’ O'Connell, a National Army general. This was a further trigger for the attack that followed.
notes.tip: Learn the order of the June events: election on 16 June, Wilson shot on 22 June, O'Connell kidnapped on 26 June, shelling on 28 June. A dated sequence earns marks.

notes.h: The Civil War begins: the Four Courts and the towns, June-August 1922
notes.b: The fighting began when the National Army attacked the Four Courts. With the better weapons, it then retook the towns, and the anti-Treaty side changed its tactics.
points: On 28 June 1922 the National Army began shelling the Four Courts with British field guns (18-pounders). The garrison surrendered on 30 June after an explosion in the Public Record Office destroyed many records.
Fighting in Dublin ended in early July. Cathal Brugha was fatally wounded on 5 July and died on 7 July 1922.
The National Army held the larger forces and better arms, and it relied on British guns and supplies, which the anti-Treaty IRA could not match.
It took Limerick and Waterford in July, and landed at Fenit, Co. Kerry, on 2 August and at Passage West, Cork, on 8 August 1922.
By the end of August the anti-Treaty side had lost the main towns, so it turned to guerrilla warfare: ambushes and the destruction of roads, bridges and railways.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, give dates for the Four Courts: occupation on 14 April, shelling on 28 June and surrender on 30 June. Each correct, dated fact earns a mark.

notes.h: The deaths of Griffith and Collins, August 1922
notes.b: Within ten days the pro-Treaty side lost both of its leaders. The government that was left was led by new men with a harder line.
points: Arthur Griffith died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922.
Michael Collins was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth, Co. Cork, on 22 August 1922. By then he was commander-in-chief of the National Army, a post he took only in July, after the war began.
Mulcahy became commander-in-chief, and Cosgrave became head of the government as chairman of the Provisional Government. In December he became President of the Executive Council.
Cosgrave and Mulcahy took charge after Collins's death.
notes.tip: State only that Collins was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth on 22 August 1922. Do not say who fired the shot.

notes.b: As the guerrilla war dragged on, the government decided to use the law and the firing squad to break it. These executions were the most bitter memory of the war.
points: The Army Emergency Powers Resolution of 27 September 1922 set up military courts and made possession of arms punishable by death. It took effect from 15 October, after an amnesty.
The first four executions took place on 17 November 1922. Erskine Childers was shot on 24 November for possessing a small pistol.
On 8 December 1922 Rory O'Connor, Liam Mellows, Joe McKelvey and Dick Barrett were executed in reprisal for the killing of the TD Seán Hales the day before.
In total the Free State executed about 80 anti-Treaty prisoners. The figures given are between 77 and 81 depending on the source, so the safe way to give it is ‘about 80’.
The executions, along with the emergency law, were the main complaint of the government's critics, who described them as repression.
notes.tip: Give the executions in order, with the reason for the 8 December killings (reprisal for Hales). Say ‘about 80’ in total, not an exact number.

notes.h: Reprisals and the end of the war, 1923
notes.b: By 1923 the war was a grim guerrilla struggle. Atrocities by the National Army hardened opinion, but the anti-Treaty leadership was running out of men and places to fight from.
points: At Ballyseedy, Co. Kerry, on 7 March 1923, prisoners were tied to a mine, which National Army soldiers then detonated. Eight died and one, Stephen Fuller, survived. There were other Kerry killings the same week, and they shocked many on the pro-Treaty side as well.
Liam Lynch, the anti-Treaty chief of staff, was mortally wounded in the Knockmealdown Mountains on 10 April 1923. He died that day or the next, and 10 April is the date to use.
Frank Aiken became chief of staff, and a ceasefire began on 30 April 1923.
On 24 May 1923 Aiken ordered the anti-Treaty side to dump arms, with a message from de Valera supporting the order.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the people. Lynch was the chief of staff killed in April 1923, Aiken his successor, and Liam Mellows was executed in December 1922.

notes.h: Why the anti-Treaty side lost, and what the war cost
notes.b: The war ended in defeat for the anti-Treaty side because it lacked the support, the weapons and the territory to win. The costs were high and are still debated.
points: The anti-Treaty side lacked public support, as shown by the June 1922 election, in which pro-Treaty candidates won 58 seats and anti-Treaty candidates 36.
The Church condemned the anti-Treaty campaign, which weakened its moral claim in a deeply Catholic country.
Its arms were weaker than those of the National Army, which used British guns and supplies. It also lost the towns by the end of August 1922, leaving it with only guerrilla tactics.

Physical force (the tradition of armed struggle) was used by the anti-Treaty IRA against the Free State. The state met it with its own force and emergency law, which is why the army, the military courts and the executions were so central to the war.
The number of dead has no agreed figure. Estimates range from about 1,500 to about 4,000 or more, so give the range and not a single total.
Thousands were imprisoned, about 12,000 by the end of the war, and roads, bridges and railways had been destroyed.
notes.tip: Do not give a single death toll for the war.

notes.h: State building under Cosgrave: the Constitution and the new party
notes.b: With the war won, the government set out to build a stable state. Cumann na nGaedheal, the pro-Treaty party, set up the institutions with an emphasis on continuity, law and order.
points: Cumann na nGaedheal was founded in April 1923 (use 1923) and led by Cosgrave. It governed from 1922/23 until 1932.

The Constitution of the Irish Free State came into force on 6 December 1922, which formally established the Free State, the new self-governing state. The Executive Council is the Free State's cabinet.
The Oireachtas (parliament) was made up of the Dáil, the Seanad and the King. Elections used proportional representation by the single transferable vote (PR-STV), so smaller parties could win seats.
The Executive Council was responsible to the Dáil, which means the government could stay in office only while it had the Dáil's support.
The Governor-General was the King's representative. Members swore an oath of fidelity to the Free State and faithfulness to the King, which was the symbol the anti-Treaty side most disliked.
Tim Healy was Governor-General from 1922 to 1928, and James McNeill held the post from 1928 to 1932.
The Referendum and Initiative provisions, which gave voters a way to challenge or propose laws, were removed in 1928.
notes.tip: Keep the Provisional Government (Collins, January 1922), the Dáil government (Griffith) and the Executive Council (from December 1922, under Cosgrave) distinct. The oath is the key link between the Constitution and the later Fianna Fáil story.

notes.h: State building: the Garda, the courts and the civil service
notes.b: A new state needs a police force, courts and administrators it can trust. The government chose to build these in a way that kept as much order and continuity as it could.
points: The Civic Guard was founded in 1922 by the Provisional Government and renamed the Garda Síochána by the Garda Síochána Act 1923. It was unarmed.
Eoin O'Duffy was Commissioner from September 1922. The Dublin Metropolitan Police merged into the Garda in 1925, so there was one national police force.
The Courts of Justice Act 1924 set up the District Court, Circuit Court, High Court and Supreme Court, replacing both the British-era courts and the Dáil courts.
The civil service and local-government system were largely inherited from British rule, which gave the new state continuity and efficiency.
The Ministers and Secretaries Act 1924 set out the government departments.
notes.tip: For short answers, remember that the Garda Síochána was unarmed and dates from 1923, with the Civic Guard as its predecessor in 1922.

notes.h: State building: standing abroad, land and electricity
notes.b: The government also won recognition abroad and tackled land and power. These were practical achievements that gave the state credibility.
points: The Free State joined the League of Nations in September 1923 and opened a legation (a small embassy) in Washington in 1924, which showed that it was accepted as a state in its own right.
The Land Act 1923, brought in by the Minister for Agriculture Patrick Hogan, completed the transfer of land to tenants by compulsory purchase of untenanted land.

The Shannon Scheme was approved in 1925 under the Minister for Industry and Commerce, Patrick McGilligan, and was built by Siemens-Schuckert of Germany. It harnessed the river Shannon to produce electricity.
The Electricity Supply Board (ESB) was created in 1927, and the Ardnacrusha power station opened in 1929, which gave the state a national electricity supply.
notes.tip: Short answers on a document often ask about the Shannon Scheme: give Ardnacrusha, 1929, the ESB and the German firm.

notes.b: The first serious test after the war came from inside the army. It showed whether elected ministers or armed officers would decide the state's policy.
points: The Army Mutiny of March 1924 was led by Liam Tobin and Charles Dalton, former IRA and IRB officers who had been Collins's intelligence men.
They objected to demobilisation (the reduction of the army after the war) and to ex-British army officers in the National Army, whom they distrusted.
Mulcahy resigned as Minister for Defence and the Army Council resigned. Kevin O'Higgins took charge of reorganising the army.
The result was that the army was firmly under civilian control.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Army Mutiny of 1924 with the Civil War. Explain it as a threat: who, what, date, the government's response and the outcome.

notes.h: Threat: the Boundary Commission crisis, November-December 1925
notes.b: The Treaty had promised a Boundary Commission, and nationalists hoped it would move the border in their favour. In 1925 those hopes collapsed and the government faced a political crisis.
points: The Morning Post published the expected findings of the Boundary Commission on 7 November 1925.
Eoin MacNeill, the Free State's member, resigned from the Commission on 20 November, which deepened the crisis.
The Tripartite Agreement of 3 December 1925, between Britain, the Free State and Northern Ireland, left the border unchanged and freed the Free State of its share of the British public debt.
The Boundary Commission, set up under the Treaty in 1924-25, was ended by the Tripartite Agreement.
notes.tip: Keep the Boundary Commission (1924-25) and the Tripartite Agreement (3 December 1925, which ended it) separate.

notes.h: Threat: Kevin O'Higgins, the Public Safety Acts and the assassination of 1927
notes.b: The government's main answer to armed opposition was emergency law, and its leading figure was Kevin O'Higgins. His murder in 1927 brought the state to a turning point.
points: Kevin O'Higgins (born 1892) was Vice-President of the Executive Council and Minister for Justice (and External Affairs).
The Public Safety (Emergency Powers) Act 1923 gave the government special powers against armed opposition.
O'Higgins was shot dead on 10 July 1927 at Booterstown, on his way to Mass, by three anti-Treaty IRA men acting without the authority of the IRA leadership.

After the murder the government introduced the Public Safety Act 1927 and the Electoral Amendment Act 1927, which required candidates to swear to take the oath if elected or be disqualified from standing.

The Constitution (Amendment No. 17) Act 1931 added Article 2A, which allowed military tribunals, and Saor Éire and the IRA were declared unlawful in October 1931. This was the last of the emergency measures of this period.
notes.tip: For a threats question, explain each threat as a threat (who, what, date), then the response and the outcome. Do not just list events.

notes.h: Consolidating democracy: Fianna Fáil enters the Dáil
notes.b: The anti-Treaty side could not win by force, so its main political leader changed course. Constitutional republicanism, led by de Valera, replaced armed resistance.
points: De Valera left Sinn Féin in March 1926 after its Ard Fheis (annual conference) refused to drop abstention, the policy of not taking seats in the Dáil.
Fianna Fáil was founded on 16 May 1926 at the La Scala Theatre, Dublin. De Valera called the oath ‘an empty political formula’, so it could be sworn in order to enter the Dáil.
In the June 1927 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 47 seats and Fianna Fáil 44. In the September 1927 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 62 and Fianna Fáil 57.

Fianna Fáil TDs signed the oath book and entered the Dáil on 12 August 1927, under the threat of the Electoral Amendment Act. If they had refused, they would have been disqualified, so they had to choose between entering the Dáil and leaving politics.
By entering the Dáil, the main opposition accepted the Free State's parliamentary system, which gave the state legitimacy.
notes.tip: Do not give an exact date for the Electoral Amendment Act. Say Fianna Fáil entered the Dáil on 12 August 1927 under the threat of it.

notes.h: Consolidating democracy: the transfer of power in 1932
notes.b: The real test of democracy came when the government that won the war lost an election. In 1932 power passed peacefully to the other side of the Civil War.
points: The world Depression from 1929 and falling farm prices hurt the Free State. Cumann na nGaedheal's cuts and balanced budgets lost it support.
Fianna Fáil promised protective tariffs, an end to the land annuity payments to Britain and the removal of the oath.
In the February 1932 general election Fianna Fáil won 72 seats, Cumann na nGaedheal 57 and Labour 7.
De Valera was elected President of the Executive Council on 9 March 1932 with Labour support.
Cosgrave's government handed over power peacefully, and the army and police accepted the change. This was the first democratic transfer of power in the new state, just nine years after a civil war.
notes.tip: The peaceful handover of 1932 is the usual climax of an essay. Explain it as a test of democracy, with the reasons why the army and police accepted it.

notes.b: The war ended in 1923, but its effects lasted much longer. It shaped the party system and left memories that many people preferred not to discuss.
points: The two sides became the two main parties. Fine Gael was formed in 1933 from Cumann na nGaedheal, the Centre Party and the Blueshirts, with Eoin O'Duffy as first leader. Fianna Fáil came from the anti-Treaty side.
In the August 1923 election Cumann na nGaedheal won 63 seats and the republicans (Sinn Féin) 44. The republicans abstained, so they did not take their seats.
De Valera was arrested at Ennis on 15 August 1923 and released on 16 July 1924.
Thousands of republican prisoners were held. A hunger strike from October to November 1923 ended without success, and two prisoners died.

Both sides committed atrocities, and families and communities were divided, because neighbours and relatives had fought on opposite sides, and this made the war a subject of silence in Irish public life.
notes.tip: Remember that Cosgrave was not the first leader of Fine Gael. O'Duffy was, and Cosgrave led it from 1935 to 1944.

notes.b: Cosgrave led the pro-Treaty side from 1922 to 1932 and built the state's institutions. He is judged as a cautious administrator who secured democracy but did little about the Depression.
points: William Thomas Cosgrave was born in Dublin on 6 June 1880, the son of a publican in James's Street. He was a Sinn Féin member of Dublin Corporation from 1909.
In 1916 he was in the South Dublin Union garrison. His death sentence was commuted to penal servitude.
He won the Kilkenny City by-election in August 1917 and was Minister for Local Government in the Dáil ministry from April 1919.
He became head of the government in August 1922, as chairman of the Provisional Government, and was President of the Executive Council from 6 December 1922 to 9 March 1932.

As a participant, he led the government through the Civil War executions, the Mutiny, the Boundary Commission crisis, the assassination of O'Higgins and the 1932 handover. The war and the killings of Hales and O'Higgins pushed him toward harsher measures.
His cautious style suited a state that needed stability, but it was less suited to the Depression.

Contemporaries: supporters admired his honesty and defence of law and stability, but critics called him conservative and authoritarian, described his government as ‘the Treaty government’, and attacked the executions, the emergency laws and economic conservatism.

Historians: Tom Garvin (1922: The Birth of Irish Democracy, 1996) praises him for defending democracy against militarism, while John M. Regan (The Irish Counter-Revolution, 1921-1936, 1999) calls the government a conservative, elitist counter-revolution. Michael Laffan (Judging W.T. Cosgrave, 2014) gives a balanced assessment.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, use four or five specific points: 1909, 1916, 1917, 1922-32, and what his government did (Garda, Mutiny, Shannon Scheme, O'Higgins), then add a judgement. Note he led Fine Gael from 1935 to 1944, retired from the Dáil in 1944 and died on 16 November 1965.

notes.h: Assessment: the Cosgrave governments' achievements and limits
notes.b: Judgements depend on whether the test is survival and legitimacy or social and economic performance. Examiners reward paired points: achievements against limits, and contemporary against later views.
points: Achievement: the state survived civil war, mutiny and assassination, and had working institutions by 1927, such as the Garda, the courts and the civil service.
Achievement: the army was brought under civil control after the Mutiny of 1924, which meant the state's policy would be decided by elected ministers.
Achievement: the Shannon Scheme and the ESB gave the state a modern electricity system.
Achievement: the peaceful transfer of power in 1932, accepted by the army and police, showed that democratic institutions had become accepted.
Limit: the government used military courts, executions and public safety laws that opponents described as repression.

Limit: its economic conservatism, based on low spending and balanced budgets, did little for the Depression's hardship, and the Boundary Commission outcome of 1925 showed that hopes of the Treaty on the north were unrealistic. The Treaty symbols, the oath and the Governor-General, were also left in place.
Contemporary view: supporters saw the government as the defender of law and stability, while opponents called it ‘the Treaty government’.
Later view: historians disagree over whether it was a successful counter to militarism (Garvin) or a conservative counter-revolution (Regan).
notes.tip: Open with a clear thesis: the state survived and democracy took root, with limits. Back each point with dated evidence, and name Garvin or Regan with the point he makes.

keyTerms.definition: The pro-Treaty government chaired by Collins from January 1922 until the Free State was established in December 1922.
The conflict between the pro-Treaty National Army and the anti-Treaty IRA from June 1922 to May 1923.
The dominion created by the Treaty and the 1922 Constitution, in existence from 6 December 1922.
The form of state demanded by the anti-Treaty side, which refused to accept the Crown and the oath.
The tradition of armed struggle, which the anti-Treaty IRA continued after 1922 against the Free State.
The Treaty status of the Free State as a self-governing member of the Commonwealth.
The pro-Treaty party founded in 1923 that governed until 1932.
The unarmed police force created in 1922 as the Civic Guard and renamed in 1923.
Laws, notably in 1923 and 1927, giving the government emergency powers against armed opposition.
The law requiring election candidates to pledge to take their seats, which in effect forced Fianna Fáil to take the oath.
The party founded by de Valera in May 1926 that entered the Dáil in 1927 and won power in 1932.
The hydroelectric project at Ardnacrusha on the Shannon, begun in 1925 and opened in 1929, run by the ESB from 1927.
